modules.title: 1 · The line of best fit
modules.summary: What OLS does, and recovering a known slope from data.

stages.title: Modelling y with a line
stages.html:
The line of best fit

Econometrics starts here. We model an outcome y as a straight-line function of a regressor x, plus an error ε for everything we didn't measure:

y = β₀ + β₁·x + ε

β₀ is the intercept and β₁ is the slope — the effect on y of a one-unit change in x. Ordinary Least Squares (OLS) chooses the β's that make the line as close to the points as possible.

Key idea. OLS minimises the sum of squared vertical gaps between the points and the line: Σ(yᵢ − ŷᵢ)².

stages.title: Estimate it
stages.note: We simulate data with a true intercept of 2 and slope of 3, then check that statsmodels recovers them.
stages.code:
import numpy as np, statsmodels.api as sm
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
n = 200
x = rng.normal(0, 1, n)
y = 2 + 3 * x + rng.normal(0, 1, n)        # truth: β0=2, β1=3

res = sm.OLS(y, sm.add_constant(x)).fit()
print(res.summary())

plt.figure(figsize=(6, 3.7))
plt.scatter(x, y, s=12, color="#da9100", alpha=0.5)
xs = np.linspace(x.min(), x.max(), 50)
plt.plot(xs, res.params[0] + res.params[1] * xs, color="#c9c6ac", lw=2)
plt.xlabel("x"); plt.ylabel("y")
plt.title(f"intercept={res.params[0]:.2f}, slope={res.params[1]:.2f}")

stages.title: Feel the fit
stages.note: Drag the sliders. Watch the line, the estimated slope, and its standard error react in real time — more noise means a fuzzier, less certain estimate.
stages.template:
import numpy as np, statsmodels.api as sm, matplotlib.pyplot as plt
rng = np.random.default_rng(0); n = 200
x = rng.normal(0, 1, n)
y = 2 + {{slope}} * x + rng.normal(0, {{noise}}, n)
res = sm.OLS(y, sm.add_constant(x)).fit()
plt.figure(figsize=(6, 3.7))
plt.scatter(x, y, s=12, color="#da9100", alpha=0.5)
xs = np.linspace(x.min(), x.max(), 50)
plt.plot(xs, res.params[0] + res.params[1]*xs, color="#c9c6ac", lw=2)
plt.title(f"beta1_hat = {res.params[1]:.2f}   SE = {res.bse[1]:.3f}")

stages.title: Check
stages.prompt: Holding n fixed, doubling the noise σ does what to the slope's standard error?
stages.hint: The standard error of β̂₁ is proportional to σ.
stages.explain: SE(β̂₁) ∝ σ, so doubling σ roughly doubles the standard error — the slider shows exactly this.

stages.title: Does a great fit prove the cause?
stages.prompt: You just fit the line and read off the summary. Claim: a regression with R² = 0.92 has clearly captured the causal effect of the regressor on y.
stages.hint: R² measures in-sample fit. Does fit say anything about whether x is correlated with the error?
stages.explain: This is the high-R²-is-causal trap. R² is only the fraction of in-sample variance the line reproduces — it says nothing about bias, omitted variables, or causation. A confounded regression (ability omitted from wage~schooling) can sit at R²≈0.9, while a perfectly unbiased causal estimate can have R²≈0.1. Boundary: R² and t-stats describe fit and noise; a causal claim needs E[ε|x]=0, which no in-sample statistic can certify. Whenever a defence of causality cites R² or a t-stat, suspect this error.

modules.title: 2 · How OLS finds the line
modules.summary: The normal equations — OLS in one line of linear algebra.

stages.title: The normal equations
stages.html:
Where the estimate comes from

Stack the data into a matrix X (a column of 1s for the intercept, then x) and a vector y. Minimising the squared residuals has a famous closed-form solution, the normal equations:

β̂ = (XᵀX)⁻¹ Xᵀy

That single formula is OLS. statsmodels computes it (more carefully, via a stable decomposition), but the result is identical.

stages.title: Compute β̂ by hand vs statsmodels
stages.note: Solve the normal equations with NumPy and confirm it matches sm.OLS exactly.
stages.code:
import numpy as np, statsmodels.api as sm
rng = np.random.default_rng(0); n = 100
x = rng.normal(0, 1, n)
y = 1 + 2 * x + rng.normal(0, 1, n)
X = sm.add_constant(x)

beta_manual = np.linalg.solve(X.T @ X, X.T @ y)   # (X'X)^{-1} X'y
beta_sm = sm.OLS(y, X).fit().params

print("normal equations :", beta_manual.round(4))
print("statsmodels      :", beta_sm.round(4))

stages.title: Check
stages.prompt: In β̂ = (XᵀX)⁻¹Xᵀy, what does the column of 1s in X provide?
stages.hint: Think about what a constant regressor estimates.
stages.explain: The constant (column of 1s) lets the model estimate the intercept β₀.

stages.title: Is β̂ unbiased for the causal return?
stages.prompt: You just computed β̂ = (XᵀX)⁻¹Xᵀy. For wage on schooling it returns β̂ = 0.08 with R² = 0.31 and t = 9.2. This β̂ is unbiased for the causal return to schooling…
choices: …yes, because R² = 0.31 shows the model fits well
…only if schooling is uncorrelated with the error (e.g. unobserved ability)
why: A big t-stat is about sampling noise, not bias — the formula (XᵀX)⁻¹Xᵀy is exact regardless of significance.
Fit ≠ identification — this is the omitted-variable trap; R² can be high while β̂ is badly confounded.
Homoskedasticity affects only the standard errors, not whether β̂ is unbiased.
stages.hint: The normal equations always return a number. Unbiasedness is a separate condition: E[ε|x]=0.
stages.explain: This is the fit-vs-identification trap. The formula β̂ = (XᵀX)⁻¹Xᵀy mechanically produces an estimate no matter what — unbiasedness for the causal effect needs E[ε|x]=0. Unobserved ability lives in ε and correlates with schooling, so β̂ is biased upward regardless of t or R². Boundary: t and R² certify nothing about exogeneity — that gap is exactly why instrumental variables exist.

modules.title: 3 · Inference
modules.summary: Standard errors, t-statistics, confidence intervals — and how they shrink with n.

stages.title: From estimate to uncertainty
stages.html:
How sure are we?

An estimate β̂₁ is useless without a sense of its uncertainty. The standard error measures that; the t-statistic (β̂ ⁄ SE) tests whether the true coefficient is zero; the 95% confidence interval is roughly β̂ ± 2·SE.

Key idea. Precision improves with the square root of the sample size: SE shrinks like 1⁄√n. Four times the data ⇒ half the standard error.

stages.title: Read the inference
stages.note: The summary's coef / std err / t / P>|t| / [0.025 0.975] columns are exact statsmodels inference.
stages.code:
import numpy as np, statsmodels.api as sm
rng = np.random.default_rng(0); n = 120
x = rng.normal(0, 1, n)
y = 1 + 2 * x + rng.normal(0, 1.5, n)
res = sm.OLS(y, sm.add_constant(x)).fit()
print(res.summary().tables[1])
print("\nslope:", round(float(res.params[1]), 3),
      "| SE:", round(float(res.bse[1]), 3),
      "| 95% CI:", np.round(res.conf_int()[1], 3))

stages.title: More data, more certainty
stages.note: Increase n and watch the 95% interval for the slope tighten around the truth (2.0).
stages.template:
import numpy as np, statsmodels.api as sm, matplotlib.pyplot as plt
rng = np.random.default_rng(0); n = {{n}}; sd = {{noise}}
x = rng.normal(0, 1, n)
y = 1 + 2 * x + rng.normal(0, sd, n)
res = sm.OLS(y, sm.add_constant(x)).fit()
lo, hi = res.conf_int()[1]
b = res.params[1]
plt.figure(figsize=(6, 3.7))
plt.errorbar([0], [b], yerr=[[b - lo], [hi - b]], fmt="o", color="#da9100", capsize=8, lw=2)
plt.axhline(2, color="#af983f", ls="--", lw=1)
plt.ylim(0, 4); plt.xlim(-1, 1); plt.xticks([])
plt.ylabel("beta1 estimate  ±95% CI")
plt.title(f"n={n}   SE={res.bse[1]:.3f}")

stages.title: Check
stages.prompt: To halve a coefficient's standard error, you should multiply the sample size by about…
stages.explain: Because SE shrinks like 1⁄√n, you need 4× the data to halve it.

stages.title: What does 'explained' mean?
stages.prompt: The inference summary reports R² = 0.36. What percent of the in-sample variance in y does the model account for? Enter a number, no % sign.
stages.hint: R² is already a fraction of variance — just convert 0.36 to a percent.
stages.explain: 36%. This defuses the word 'explained': R² literally equals the fraction of sample variance reproduced in this sample — 'explained' here is statistical bookkeeping, not a causal claim. The tempting move is to hear 'explains 36% of y' as 'causes 36% of y'; that fails because R² is silent about bias. Boundary: 36% explained is fully compatible with a biased slope, and 99% is compatible with a hopelessly confounded one.

stages.title: How much data to halve the SE?
stages.prompt: You saw SE shrink like 1⁄√n. Starting from a sample of n = 250, by what factor must you multiply n to halve the slope's standard error? Enter the factor (a plain number).
stages.hint: SE ∝ 1⁄√n, so halving SE means doubling √n. What does that do to n itself?
stages.explain: This catches the linear-precision trap — assuming twice the data halves the SE. Because SE ∝ 1⁄√n, halving the SE requires doubling √n, which means multiplying n by 2² = 4. So n goes 250 → 1000. Boundary: the √n law makes precision expensive — each further halving of the SE costs another 4× in data, which is why huge samples buy ever less extra certainty.

modules.title: 4 · Assumptions & diagnostics
modules.summary: Gauss–Markov, heteroskedasticity, and robust standard errors.

stages.title: When is OLS trustworthy?
stages.html:
The fine print

OLS is unbiased when the error is mean-zero and uncorrelated with x. It is the most efficient linear unbiased estimator (Gauss–Markov) when the errors also have constant variance (homoskedasticity) and are uncorrelated.

Real data often violate constant variance — the spread of y grows with x (heteroskedasticity). OLS estimates stay unbiased, but the standard errors are wrong. The fix is robust (HC) standard errors.

stages.title: Spot heteroskedasticity, then fix the SEs
stages.note: Residuals that fan out signal heteroskedasticity; HC1 robust SEs correct the inference.
stages.code:
import numpy as np, statsmodels.api as sm
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

rng = np.random.default_rng(0); n = 300
x = rng.uniform(0, 3, n)
y = 1 + 2 * x + rng.normal(0, 0.4 + 0.9 * x, n)   # variance grows with x

res = sm.OLS(y, sm.add_constant(x)).fit()
res_robust = res.get_robustcov_results(cov_type="HC1")
print("classical SE:", np.round(res.bse, 3))
print("robust  SE :", np.round(res_robust.bse, 3))

plt.figure(figsize=(6, 3.7))
plt.scatter(x, res.resid, s=12, color="#da9100", alpha=0.5)
plt.axhline(0, color="#c9c6ac", lw=1)
plt.xlabel("x"); plt.ylabel("residual")
plt.title("Residuals fan out → heteroskedasticity")

stages.title: Check
stages.prompt: Under heteroskedasticity, ordinary OLS gives you…
stages.hint: Heteroskedasticity is about the variance of the error, not its mean.
stages.explain: Coefficients remain unbiased; only the standard errors are wrong — use robust (HC) SEs.

stages.title: Does heteroskedasticity bias the coefficients?
stages.prompt: You just saw the residuals fan out with x. Claim: heteroskedasticity biases the OLS coefficients, so you must drop the affected observations.
stages.hint: Heteroskedasticity changes the error's variance, not its mean. Which OLS property depends on the mean of the error?
stages.explain: This is the heteroskedasticity-biases-coefficients trap. Heteroskedasticity is about the variance of the error, not its mean — so unbiasedness (which needs E[ε|x]=0) is untouched; β̂ stays unbiased and only the default standard errors are wrong. The tempting fix — deleting data — throws away valid information and introduces selection bias. Boundary: the right fix is robust (HC1) standard errors, which correct the inference while leaving the unbiased coefficients in place.

stages.title: What does heteroskedasticity actually break?
stages.prompt: Residuals fan out with x. Select all that apply: which statements about OLS under heteroskedasticity are TRUE?
choices: The coefficient estimates β̂ remain unbiased
The default (classical) standard errors are wrong
Robust (HC1) standard errors fix the inference
The coefficient estimates β̂ become biased
You should delete the high-variance observations to fix it
stages.hint: Separate what changes (the variance of the error, hence the SEs) from what doesn't (the mean of the error, hence unbiasedness).
stages.explain: This re-plants the heteroskedasticity-biases-coefficients trap as a set. TRUE: β̂ stays unbiased (it needs E[ε|x]=0, untouched by non-constant variance), the classical SEs are wrong, and robust HC1 SEs repair the inference. FALSE distractors: 'β̂ becomes biased' is the central misconception — variance is not bias; and 'delete the high-variance observations' discards valid data and induces selection bias. Boundary: heteroskedasticity costs you efficiency and correct SEs, never unbiasedness.
